Here's the first question: "Tell me about a time you analyzed a complex financial problem and how your analysis changed a decision or outcome."

Score: 2/10.
- Structure 1/4: You gave the action but not the Situation/Task or a clear Result.

You don't have a resume on file here yet. I can still help: tell me whether you want feedback for Junior Software Engineer roles in general, or for a specific posting or city. Default I’ll assume general junior SWE in the US and give a focused checklist and quick edits you can make now.

Assuming general junior SWE (US), here’s what most hiring teams look for and what to add or improve on a resume:

1) Contact + GitHub/LinkedIn visible and active
- What to include: name, email, city (or remote), phone, GitHub link, LinkedIn, portfolio/website if any.
- Make sure GitHub has recent commits and at least 2–3 polished projects with README, instructions, and live demo or screenshots.
2) Short summary or objective (1 line)
- One crisp line: your title, years (or “career switch”), and target (“seeking Junior Software Engineer roles focused on [backend/frontend/full‑stack]”).

3) Technical skills section (clear, scannable)
- Languages: list main ones (e.g., Python, Java, JavaScript/TypeScript, C#).
- Frameworks/tools: React, Node, Django, Spring, etc.
- Databases, testing, CI/CD, cloud (AWS/GCP), containerization (Docker), and any relevant libraries.
- Put skills in order of strength and relevance to roles you want.
4) Projects (actionable, measurable, focused)
- Include 2–4 projects (not just coursework). For each:
  - Title + link (GitHub/live) + tech stack.
  - 2–3 bullet points: what you built, your specific contributions, and one result/metric (users, performance improvement, tests added, API response time, or a demo link).
  - Emphasize code quality, tests, deployment, and teamwork if applicable.
5) Experience (internships, freelance, relevant work)
- For each role: employer, title, dates, 2–4 bullets.
- Use STAR-style: problem → what you did (tech + ownership) → measurable result (reduced latency by X%, improved coverage to Y%, shipped feature used by N users).
- If you lack professional SWE experience, convert non-software roles into engineering-relevant bullets (automation, scripting, data analysis, teamwork, CI/CD).

6) Education + credentials
- Degree, school, graduation date (or "expected"), GPA only if strong and recent.
- Add relevant coursework only if early in career (data structures, algorithms, systems).
- List certs (AWS, relevant bootcamps) if recent.
7) Algorithms & CS fundamentals evidence
- Mention coursework, projects or interview prep (LeetCode practice, coding challenge results) and any open-source contributions.
- If you have passed coding tests or platform ranks, note them briefly.

8) Tests, quality, delivery signals
- Note unit/integration tests, TDD, code reviews, CI pipelines, deployment experience.
- Hiring teams want evidence you can ship and maintain code.

9) Tailoring & keywords
- Mirror wording from job descriptions: e.g., “REST APIs”, “React hooks”, “OAuth2”, “SQL/noSQL”.
- For each application, tailor the top 6 bullets and the skills list.
10) Formatting & length
- One page preferred for junior roles; two only if you have substantial relevant experience.
- Use clear headings, bullet points, consistent tense.
- ATS-safe: avoid headers/footers with contact info only; use plain text for skills and tech.
Quick specific edits to make right now (apply these to your resume draft):
- Add a GitHub link and ensure 2 projects have README + demo.
- For one project, change a vague bullet like “Built a web app” to “Built a React + Node app with JWT auth and PostgreSQL; implemented REST API and Dockerized deployment; added 80% test coverage—deployed to Heroku with 250 weekly users.”
- Replace “Worked on backend” with “Implemented CRUD endpoints in Express, optimized DB queries to reduce response time by 40%.”
- Add a short 1-line objective: “Junior Software Engineer with hands-on experience in React and Node; seeking entry-level backend/full-stack roles.”
One next step: paste your resume text (or upload it) here and I will read it, save each entry, then give a 2–3 line summary of what I read (latest role, top skills, education), two concrete changes to improve it for Junior SWE roles, and offer to search for matching jobs. Is that what you want?

replies:
Accounting first, then valuation and M&A, then behavioral — short drills you can run now and a 20‑minute mock you can do out loud.
What the interview will ask (top areas)
- Accounting basics: three‑statement link, working capital mechanics, depreciation vs capex, deferred tax basics.
- Valuation / modeling: DCF steps and main drivers, comps (how you pick and adjust multiples), quick sensitivity logic.
- M&A / deal sense: sell‑side vs buy‑side process, accretion/dilution intuition, purchase price allocation and basic integration risks.
- Fit / behavioral: Tell me about yourself; teamwork; a time you missed something; how you handle heavy deadlines.
- Technical case: short live modeling or a valuation exercise (walk through assumptions and show your logic).
Two‑minute checklist for the day before
- Ask the recruiter for the job description and names/titles of interviewers; if they won’t share names, ask for rounds/topics.
- Re‑read deals/models on your resume and pull one or two exact metrics (deal size, % change, weeks saved).
- Test Zoom/Teams link, camera, mic; have a printed resume and the JD beside you.
- Prepare two tailored questions to ask (see examples below).
60–75s “Tell me about yourself” structure (use concrete metrics)
- 1 line current role + top deliverable.
- 1–2 lines 2–3 achievements most relevant to an M&A analyst (models built, deals supported, key outcomes).
- 1 line why Lincoln International and what you’ll bring (tie to mid‑market execution or sector focus).
Template you should adapt
- “I’m [current title] at [firm], where I build and quality‑check financial models and supported [X] transactions — most recently I [concise achievement with metric]. I enjoy transaction execution and client work; at Lincoln I want to work on [mid‑market / sector] deals and bring disciplined modeling and concise client deliverables so deals move faster.”

Three behavioral stories to prepare (one line prompts)
- Team win: context → your role → action you led → numeric result.
- Hard problem: what the obstacle was → how you structured the solution → what changed.
- Failure/missed issue: own the mistake → corrective steps → what you changed going forward.
Precise technical drills (time yourself)
- Accounting drill (60–90s): “If revenue increases by $X, what happens to the three statements?” Say the P&L impact, tax, balance sheet (AR) and cash flow (NWC), and mention capex if growth implies it.
- DCF drill (90s): “Walk me through a DCF.” Say project unlevered FCF, pick discount rate (WACC) and terminal value approach, discount, create sensitivity table — and name the biggest drivers.
- Valuation contrast (90s): “Why use EV/EBITDA vs P/E?” Explain EV captures debt and is capital‑structure neutral; P/E is equity only and affected by leverage and taxes.
- M&A quick: “Walk me through a sell‑side process” — target prep → marketing → buyer Q&A → bids → negotiation → close/integration; and explain what makes a deal accretive vs dilutive at a high level.
Example behavioral answers — short rewrite for clarity
- Team win (structure): “On a sell‑side process for a mid‑market industrial client (S), I led cleanup of the financial model and created 3 scenario outputs for buyers (T). I standardized working‑capital templates and delivered the valuation pack one week early (A). Result: shortened buyer Q&A by [specific % or time] and supported a higher final bid (R).”
- Missed item (structure): Situation → your responsibility → immediate fixes → long‑term prevention (checklist / peer review).
Two good questions to ask them
- “What types of transactions does the team expect this year and which industries are you prioritizing?”
- “How are analyst responsibilities split between modeling, client materials, and diligence on a typical deal?”

20‑minute timed mock (do it alone or with a friend)
- 0–2 min: Tell me about yourself (60–75s).
- 2–6 min: Accounting drill — walk through three‑statements and one NWC example.
- 6–12 min: Valuation drill — walk through a DCF and what moves valuation most.
- 12–17 min: Behavioral story — pick team win with metrics.
- 17–20 min: Ask your two questions to the interviewer.
One quick day‑of interview script
- 30–60 minutes before: test tech, have resume/JD, water, print of your 3 stories and key deal numbers.
- When they open: brief smile, mirror interviewer’s energy, open with your 60s pitch, then ask if they’d like you to start with a quick summary of your deal experience.
- If given a modeling prompt you’re unsure on: state assumptions clearly, walk stepwise logic, and narrate your approximation.
What I can do next (pick one)
- Run a timed mock for “Analyst at Lincoln International” and score each answer with one concrete fix — say “mock me” and give your opening 60–75s answer out loud.
- Or: draft a 60–75s “Tell me about yourself” using the deals and numbers on your resume — paste the resume or the 2–3 deal lines you want included.

I don’t yet have your resume or the job description on file; I assumed you want a concise, execution‑focused tone with metriced examples. Which next step: run the mock now, or paste the two deal bullets I should use to write your 60–75s pitch?
